hints: Look closely at what a vaccine actually gives you: a harmless form of antigen, not ready-made antibodies. Ask yourself, who has to do the work to make the antibodies, you or the vaccine?

Remember the two pairs for immunity: natural vs artificial (did you get it by infection or by medical intervention?) and active vs passive (did your own lymphocytes make memory cells or did you just borrow antibodies?).
walkthrough:
**What does a vaccine do?**

Think of a vaccine as a safe practice run. It introduces a weakened, dead or part antigen so your body notices it without getting seriously ill.

Your own B and T lymphocytes must then respond to that antigen.

**Check statements 1 and 3**

Because your lymphocytes are stimulated, they divide, form memory cells and plasma cells release antibodies. Those antibodies and memory cells then protect you against a real future infection.

So both statement 1 (production of antibodies for future protection) and statement 3 (stimulation of appropriate lymphocytes) are true.

**Check statement 2, active or passive?**

Active means YOU make the antibodies and memory. Passive means you are GIVEN antibodies. Artificial means it comes from human medical action, not from natural infection.

Vaccination is given by humans but you make your own response, so it is artificial active immunity. Statement 2 is also true, so 1, 2 and 3 gives option A.

options.A: All three are correct. Vaccination stimulates your lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells, which is the definition of artificial active immunity.
options.B: This misses out statement 3, but stimulation of specific B and T lymphocytes is essential for making memory cells.
options.C: This misses out statement 2, but vaccination is the classic example of artificial (given medically) active (you make your own response) immunity.
options.D: This misses out statement 1, but long term protection against future infection depends on antibodies and memory cells produced after vaccination.
